title: Living faith justifies us—but is not the righteousness we stand in
source_text: VI. Quoties ergo fide justificari dicimur, id intelligendum est, non de fide mortua, sed viva, non de otiosa, sed de efficaci, ex qua nova obedientia, & bona opera prodeunt, & quae secum affert vitae totius immutationem. Porro inter Theologos Protestantes certum est fidem, etiam vivam & efficacem, non esse justitiam illam per quam coram severo Dei judicio stamus, aut justitiae illius partem vel initium. Etenim, cum fidei praecipuum officium sit ad misericordiam divinam confugere, qua ratione per eam, & illius virtute posset homo ferre rigidum justitiae divinae examen? cum repugnantia sint, egere Dei misericordia, & posse justitiam illius provocare.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore whenever we are said to be justified by faith, this is to be understood not of dead but of living faith, not of idle but of efficacious faith, from which new obedience and good works proceed, and which brings with it a change of the whole life. Further, among Protestant theologians it is certain that faith, even living and efficacious, is not that righteousness by which we stand before God's severe judgment, nor a part or beginning of that righteousness. For since faith's chief office is to flee to divine mercy, by what reason through it and by its virtue could a person bear the rigid examination of divine justice?—when to need God's mercy and to be able to challenge his justice are contradictory.
pass_b_english: Only living, efficacious faith is in view when Scripture says we are justified by faith.
Even that faith is not the righteousness we stand in before God—it flees to mercy.

lemmas.gloss: a change of the whole life
the rigid examination of divine justice

choices.why: Faith is not the formal righteousness before God.
